attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his signed Substack post.

semantics.note: The normalised proposition leaves out the second conjunct, 'Hinton knows it'. The kind (observation) is correct.

contract.note: Marcus cites Nov 25 as an example of LeCun stating the view, not as the date of the shift. Limiting 'recently' to Nov 2023–Feb 2024 is a reading he did not supply, and it decides the result. A shift around 2022 would also fit his words.

evidence.note: LeCun's Nov 2023 post shows he agrees on shallow understanding. It shows no change of view and does not show Hinton's awareness.
LeCun's Aug 2022 coauthored essay already calls LLM understanding shallow. That rules out a shift after Nov 2023, but there is no earlier baseline, so a shift before 2022 cannot be ruled out.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows LeCun agreed with Marcus by 2022 and in Nov 2023. There is no earlier statement where LeCun held a different view, so no change of position is shown either way. Nothing shows Hinton's awareness. The contract's narrow window would make e2 contradict the claim, but that window is not fair to Marcus's words.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post.

semantics.note: The compound claim is kept, and 'sometimes' qualifies the memorization part. The language is firm, not hedged.

contract.note: The plain reading of deep understanding (reliable transfer to unfamiliar cases) is ordinary and fair. The undefined threshold still decides the understanding part.

evidence.note: Nov 2023 extraction work shows long verbatim training text reproduced by ChatGPT. Supports the memorization part only.
Shows one specific failure to generalize (the reversal curse). That is not a broad finding that LLMs lack deep understanding.
Shows an emergent world representation in a synthetic Othello model. It says nothing settled about general-purpose LLMs.

reviews.rationale: The memorization part is supported by e1. The deep-understanding part is neither established nor refuted: e2 shows a narrow limitation and e3 is a synthetic case. Neither the support condition nor the contradiction condition is met for the compound claim.

semantics.note: Both parts are captured, and the scope 'some' is kept.

contract.note: Treating this as an existence claim, and reading 'subfield' as a research line with multiple studies, is an ordinary and fair reading.

evidence.note: Nov 2023 paper extracts over 10,000 verbatim training examples and reviews earlier memorization research.
Carlini et al. memorization study, revised Mar 2023 inside the target period. A separate study, which supports a continuing research line.

reviews.rationale: Experiments show training text being recovered from neural language models, and several dated studies show a sustained research line on memorization. Both parts of the claim hold.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post.

semantics.note: The claim is about the mechanisms that produce errors, so it is causal, not an observation. The narrowed car-keys comparison is faithful.

contract.note: The narrow reading (fabricating content versus ordinarily forgetting a location) matches Marcus's own example and is fair. The level at which mechanisms must differ is left open.

evidence.note: Schacter's review treats forgetting sins, including absent-mindedness, as separate from distortion sins. Supports the human side of the comparison.
Shows LLM fabrications that arise from staying consistent with earlier output, even when the model can recognize the claim as wrong. That is a different process from failing to recall.
Covers induced human false memories. That is not the car-keys case, so it is only context.

reviews.rationale: Under the narrow contract, everyday forgetting is classed as a failure of attention or retrieval, separate from distortion. The LLM fabrications documented in e2 come from a different process and produce invented content. No study compares the two directly, but nothing shows a shared mechanism, and the narrow claim is supported.
